performers: Pasquale Amato, baritone; Victor orchestra, Walter B. Rogers
intro: Escamillo answers a toast by describing the bullring, then turns the room into his audience. Pasquale Amato sings both verses in Italian: muscular minor-key storytelling, each time followed by a broad major-key refrain.

sections.label: A · A toast and a bullfight
A′ · The bull enters
sections.mNote: The minor-key narrative returns for the second verse

sections.label: B′ · The refrain returns
sections.mNote: The major-key tune closes the song

cues.title: A public voice
cues.text: Escamillo’s song starts with the orchestra’s emphatic gestures, then settles into his account of the arena. The verse stays in F minor; short repeated figures give his storytelling a clipped, physical energy.
cues.evidence: Bizet’s piano reduction, Choudens vocal score (archive.org copy catalogued 1883), no. 14, p. 128: four-flat signature, F minor, fortissimo introduction (pp. 129–130 are missing from the scan). The Toreador Song article gives the key as F minor with the refrain in F major: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toreador_Song and https://archive.org/details/carmenopracomi00bize
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: The refrain opens out
cues.text: The tune everyone remembers is in F major. Its first appearance in the score is marked softly and “avec fatuité” — with self-satisfaction. Escamillo knows the effect his refrain will have before the room joins in.
cues.evidence: Choudens vocal score (archive.org copy catalogued 1883), no. 14, p. 131: F-major refrain, piano, “avec fatuité”. The stage score adds the other characters and chorus to the refrain; this disc is a solo version. https://archive.org/details/carmenopracomi00bize
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Carmen travels in Italian
cues.text: Amato sings an Italian translation of a French opera set in Spain. His 1911 Victor disc preserves one route by which the work travelled: a star singer, an orchestra and one substantial scene on a single record side.
cues.evidence: Truesound Transfers TT-3080, track 3, prints the Italian incipit with Victor 88327, matrix C 11213-1, Victor orchestra and Walter B. Rogers. The Library of Congress National Jukebox catalogues Victor 88327, C-11213/1, as an Italian-language vocal solo with harp and orchestra recorded 9 November 1911. https://www.truesoundtransfers.de/Titellisten/TT3080.htm and https://www.loc.gov/item/jukebox-131050/

cues.title: The room remembers him
cues.text: After the second verse, the broad refrain returns. In the opera it binds Escamillo to the crowd; its later return from the bullring makes a dreadful counterpoint to Carmen and José’s private confrontation outside.
cues.evidence: Choudens vocal score (archive.org copy catalogued 1883), no. 14, from p. 137 (the refrain after the second verse), and no. 27, p. 350, where the chorus sings the refrain as Don José strikes Carmen down. The opera’s synopsis describes the same reprise: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmen and https://archive.org/details/carmenopracomi00bize
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Pasquale Amato (Escamillo, baritone), Victor orchestra (orchestral accompaniment), Francis J. Lapitino (harp), Walter B. Rogers (conductor)
fields.note: Truesound Transfers identifies the accompaniment and conductor for Victor 88327, matrix C11213-1; the Library of Congress National Jukebox lists the same performers and adds Francis J. Lapitino on harp; Commons identifies the same matrix and singer.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Italian-language solo recording, beginning Con voi ber affè mi fia caro, with orchestral accompaniment
fields.note: Both verses belong to a self-contained commercial aria side. The stage number’s ensemble responses are not represented as a complete recording of the tavern scene. The Italian translator and the precise performing edition used in the session have not been established.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The year agrees. Commons writes 11 September; the specialist discography prints 09.11.1911 in day-month-year order, meaning 9 November, and the Library of Congress National Jukebox dates the recording 1911-11-09. Only the agreed year is used in the listening header.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: No particular studio address is asserted.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: The recording circulated on several issues; no physical pressing used for the original transfer is identified.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: Victor issue identified by the specialist discography and by the Archive item title cited on Commons.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: The sources agree on C11213-1 despite their disagreement about the session’s day and month.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.value: Original transfer unidentified; noise-reduced restoration uploaded by Adam Cuerden
fields.note: Commons traces its source to Internet Archive item VrsAcoustics-88327-PasqualeAmato. That source item did not return usable metadata when consulted; no original transfer engineer is invented.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The current restored Ogg was uploaded on 16 January 2009; this is not an established date for the original disc-to-digital transfer.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: General noise reduction, followed by more selective noise removal
fields.note: The description and revision history document these operations. Stylus, playback equalisation, original sampling format and any pitch correction are not supplied. Commons also links an unrestored version.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Public-domain nineteenth-century work and historical Italian-language version
fields.note: Commons separately marks the underlying work public domain, using 1908 as the last author’s death year. Bizet’s score was published in 1875. The particular Italian translator is not identified by the recording sources; this is a historical 1911 performance, not a modern translation.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Public domain in the United States; Commons marks the commercial acoustic recording as an expired pre-cutoff sound recording
fields.note: Commons explicitly carries PD-US-record-expired and identifies a 1911 Victor recording. The identification is corroborated by the specialist discography. The licence statement does not amount to an assertion that rights are identical in every jurisdiction.

composer.epithet: A factory worker sings that love obeys no law. Beneath her voice, four bass notes keep the dance going.
facts: Paris Conservatoire; piano with Antoine Marmontel, composition with Fromental Halévy
Prix de Rome 1857 · Les Pêcheurs de perles 1863 · Carmen 1875
Jeux d’enfants for piano duet · L’Arlésienne for the spoken theatre
composer.background:
Outside the bullring, Carmen tells José that she will not return to him. Inside, the spectators cheer Escamillo. Bizet keeps both scenes audible: the tune of the Toreador Song comes through the walls while José’s pleading turns to murder. A melody that entered the opera as a public entertainment has acquired an unbearable second meaning. Carmen opened at the Paris Opéra-Comique on 3 March 1875. Three months later its composer was dead, aged thirty-six. He had spent most of his working life trying to get an opera to stay on the stage.

Georges Bizet was born in Paris on 25 October 1838. His father Adolphe taught singing; his mother Aimée played the piano, and her brother François Delsarte was a singing teacher. The boy entered the Conservatoire in October 1848, before his tenth birthday. Antoine Marmontel taught him piano, François Benoist organ, and Fromental Halévy composition. Piano, fugue and organ prizes followed. Charles Gounod became an especially important example: a composer could make a career in the theatre without giving up the suppleness of a sung phrase.
